newsitem.title: USA: Lower employee satisfaction is problem for U.S. employers.
newsitem.headline: Lower employee satisfaction is problem for U.S. employers.

text.p: Young workers who say they are very satisfied with their jobs are less likely to quit than those who are dissatisfied -- at first.

But after about four years with an employer, employees who rated their initial job satisfaction as high are "just as likely to quit as those who rated their job satisfaction as low," a new study finds.

"Job satisfaction is important initially in predicting which employees will quit, but it becomes less significant over time," said psychologist Mary Roznowski, of Ohio State University, and co-author of the study.
The study tracked 1,026 workers between 27 and 30 years of age over a four-year period. Three out of five of the workers involved in the study reportedly left their jobs within four years.
The findings pose a challenge to employers struggling to retain and motivate young employees in an increasingly volatile workplace.
"Employers need to find ways to build a sense of commitment in their workers, which is difficult these days," Roznowski said.
"Employers must be aware that job satisfaction is variable and that it does change for people," she added. "The study points to the need not to take even a seemingly satisfied employee for granted."
The subjects held a wide variety of positions ranging from machine operators to clerical and sales workers to management and administration executives.

The study data were taken from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, compiled by the Centre For Human Resource Research, in Columbus, Ohio. One job of each subject was monitored from the time it was started to the time it ended, up to four years. Those studied had to be employed at least 20 hours a week.
The subjects were asked to gauge their job satisfaction in terms of personal opportunities, workplace surroundings, income, and promotion opportunities.
"People who were initially highly satisfied with their jobs were less likely to quit than those who were less satisfied," Roznowski said.
"But the difference between the two groups grew steadily smaller until about four years later, when there was no difference between them in the likelihood of quitting," she added.
One predictor of employment longevity, Roznowski found, was that workers who scored highest on a standardised aptitude test were more likely to stay at their current job than those who scored lowest.

"Intelligent workers probably land better jobs in the first place, and find jobs that are a better fit for them, so they are less likely to leave," said Roznowski, who made the study with business administration professor David Harrison of the University of Texas at Arlington, and David Dickter, an industrial psychologist with AT&T Corp. in Plainsboro, N.J.
The high turnover rate among young workers found by the study jibe with the observations of Barry Lawrence, spokesman for the Society For Human Resource Management, of Alexandria, Va.

"That's been a problem since the beginning of time," he said. "At that age, you don't know what kind of experience you want and you have the ability more easily to switch (jobs). You don't necessarily have a huge mortgage and bills to pay."
The cost to employers of job switching, though, is heavy. "As a rule of thumb, it takes about one and a half times (the employee's) annual salary to replace that job," Lawrence said.
He went on to say that demographics indicate "you're going to see a lot of younger people entering the work force and that's going to have some interesting implications (for employers)."
Asked what advice she had for employers, Roznowski said that employees should be made to feel "they're working for the best possible company."
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
